passage:
On Saturday mornings the market hall at Ostrel smells of rind and wet stone, and for ninety years its business turned on one object: a brass beam scale at the far end of the room, facing the glass case by the hall door where the market keeps its old iron weights. A farmer would carry a wheel of cheese to the scale, the weigher would call the weight aloud, and buyer and seller would strike their bargain on that number. The buyers were village families, shopkeepers from up the valley and, lately, restaurant buyers who drive up from the city of Tessaly before dawn.

For thirty-eight years the weigher was Anselm Dray. Ask the council why the public weighing mattered and you will hear that the weighing fee, a few coins a wheel, paid for the upkeep of the hall from 1934 on. Mira Coll, a Tessaly sociologist who has studied the market for two years, calls the weighing the one habit that drew the whole valley into one room, and buyers like to say they trusted a weight they heard called aloud. Dray's answer was about the brass itself. Accounts were settled at the hall door once the weighing was done, and he liked to say that in thirty-eight years no buyer had come back to complain. “The stall scales drift with the weather,” he told me. “This one is truer than any of them.”

Dray announced his retirement two winters ago, and the council had to decide what came next. His niece, Tamsin Dray, had stood at his elbow on Saturdays since she was fourteen and had learned the scale from her uncle, down to the half-turn he gave the pan before every wheel. Odile Sarr, who chairs the council, came to its first meeting carrying the letter in which the restaurant buyers asked for a fixed price, and a sheet of her own sums showing what each cheese would fetch if the market were to price each wheel as a whole. Jory Ambel, a young goat-cheese maker, spoke for letting vendors weigh at their own stalls, and a supplier's brochure for a digital scale to replace the brass one went round the table with a quote for what it would cost to buy one.

That spring the council borrowed a digital scale for a month and set it beside the brass one. Its speed pleased almost everyone. The queue, which on busy mornings grew too long and reached the hall door, shrank to a handful of people, and the vendors who had complained of lost sales when buyers gave up and went home stopped complaining. That month an inspector from the provincial weights office tested both machines. The brass beam, he found, was out of true; worn at its pivot, it had been reading light, putting every wheel a little under its real weight.

Coll had been reading the market's sales ledgers, which go back to 1934, and after the inspector's visit she reread them. The hall's weights could be set against the weights the dairies record when a wheel leaves the press, and for at least eleven years the hall's figures had run a steady fraction under the dairies'. “It was small enough to vanish in any single sale,” Coll said. “Over a decade it was the whole margin of a small farm.” Sarr had figures of her own that summer, showing that the city restaurants had become the market's largest buyers, but it was Coll's pages the council kept returning to.

In June the council voted to buy a digital scale of its own. Tamsin, who had offered to keep the brass scale, was asked instead to run the new one, and the habits her uncle had trained into her carried over. Sarr's sums went back into her folder. What decided the vote, she said, was the inspector's report: a beam worn out of true would have to be recast, and recasting it would cost more than a new scale. The fee still pays for the upkeep of the roof, Tamsin still weighs any disputed wheel twice, and most vendors still check their cheese on their own stall scales.

I went back on a Saturday in October. The queue was short even on a busy morning. Tamsin set each wheel on the digital pan and read the figure from the screen; she still calls it aloud, out of habit, though everyone can see it. The brass scale has been moved into the glass case by the hall door, its beam wired level. The restaurant buyers, who weigh every wheel again in their kitchens, tell me the numbers now match to the gram. Waiting my turn, I caught myself looking past the screen to the case, the way you glance at a chair someone used to sit in. The lesson Ostrel took is a sound one, that a market should have its scale tested before it trusts it. I only wish the test had come out the other way.

passage:
Passage A by Mira Thessaly
For twenty years I conducted the Lamplighter's Mass as Breckholm has heard it at every performance since its premiere at Easter 1930, with the ending Piet Osker wrote after Anneliese Corran died in the winter of 1928. I used to tell choirs that Osker had faced blank paper, that the Agnus Dei was his from first bar to last, a copyist's act of nerve. When the cathedral asked me to prepare a new edition, I went to the library meaning to cut his ending and print only what Corran left.

That ending has had a long life. At the premiere Osker played the organ himself, a slight figure the newspapers did not name, and the chapter liked what it heard well enough to sing the Mass every Easter afterward. Generations of singers learned its closing pages, the tower bells ringing over the last chord, as Corran's own work. A story in the choir held that she had finished the movement and that her pages were lost, and the story made each year's performance feel like a faithful copy of something real.

In the library I found a folder of Corran's pencil sketches, eleven pages, with Osker's fair copy beside them. I went through them bar by bar. Almost every phrase I had credited to Osker sits in her pencil: the melody, the bass, even the bell part, added in her margin and circled. Her pencil runs out eight bars before his close, and those eight bars carry on the line she was tracing, in the direction she was tracing it. Tucked into the folder was Hanne Corran's letter of 1949, recalling her sister's wish that the Mass end as it began. Some colleagues have wanted to build a close from that sentence. It came twenty-one years late, and by then the pages had said more than any memory could.

A few singers asked whether we should simply stop at the last bar Corran wrote, where her pencil stops, and once, in rehearsal, I stopped the choir there. The sopranos sang Osker's last chord anyway, out of habit, and then looked at me as though I had dropped something. The new edition keeps every one of his bars, set in the same type as hers, because the join between them is a matter of handwriting more than of music. On the night the tower bells rang over the final chord as they have every Easter since 1930, and I conducted those closing pages as Corran's Mass, which, I had learned, is very nearly what they are.

Passage B by Jonah Pell
Piet Osker is usually remembered as the copyist who presumed. The record suggests a modest man with a deadline, which is a less romantic story than the legend and a more useful one. In January 1929, weeks after Corran's funeral, the cathedral chapter announced that her Mass would be sung at Easter of the following year, and Osker's first dated page of the completion is from the same month. Hanne Corran's request that he finish her sister's work arrived that autumn, when he was already copying the last movement fair. The firm of Varlow, the Breckholm publisher, took an interest only after the premiere had filled the cathedral, and the story that Osker had once heard Anneliese play the ending at her piano first appears in a memoir of 1952.

His fair copy is the best witness to how he worked. Every bar he supplied himself carries a mark in the margin, a small pencilled cross, and there are only thirty-one of them; the rest is Corran's line, copied out by a man who knew whose music he was handling. Where her pencil grows faint, he follows the faint line instead of improving on it, and where she left two chords stacked as alternatives, he copied both into the margin and chose the plainer. His letters from that year say almost nothing about the Mass, and the reviews of 1930, which praised the ending as pure Corran, show only that the seams were well hidden. The crosses show that he left them visible for anyone who cared to look.

The chapter, for its part, voted that summer to sing the Mass every Easter with Osker's ending, and it has kept that promise for most of a century. Varlow's account books show the firm buying the publishing right from Hanne, not from the chapter, in 1934; the sketches stayed in the library with the fair copy; and the tower bells that ring after the final chord were a bell-ringer's habit long before anyone wrote them down. Each Easter, Breckholm sings an ending that is more Corran's than the legend of the presumptuous copyist allows, and it owes that to thirty-one small crosses and to the man who was honest enough to make them.
